title: Audition (1999) is a stunningly complex and poignant portrayal of a basket of "man fears," and this may explain a lot of its inexplicable appeal to men in the West (spoilers inside).

commenti.body:
That was a great write-up. You definitely contextualised and explained alot of whatever I felt while watching the film and the time after it. I agree with you. I didn't think on it nearly as deeply as you did but my experience watching the film was akin to watching a thriller about a lovelife gone horribly bad.

Except that implies a woman/man being a monster and that being all the film has to offer but here alot of it are these fears that you mentioned. I love the reveal at the end so much because it feels like such a nightmare come to life than anything else. It also acted as comeuppance of sorts for the protagonist choosing and filtering women out the way he did. Like you mentioned, how he deliberately chose to ignore the nuances and weight of a relationship, instead believing it to be a trivial and easy affair.

I need to rewatch this film sometime soon, gone too long without watching it again. But weirdly it reminded me of Cure (partly because I don't think I've the film vocabularly required to reference something else xD) but they both instilled in me this base feeling of creeping, existential unease - anything seems possible.

Thanks - it's not every day that I have the energy to effortpost like this, but Miike at his best demands it.

The "comeuppance" interpretation comes up a lot as the primary justification for the film being a feminist one, but I have to wonder where people's senses of proportion are with that; this isn't I Spit On Your Grave or any other film of its kind, where the justification for female brutality in the latter half of the film is created with male brutality in the former. Shigeharu isn't paying any moral debts through his ordeal; he's paying for getting himself into a bad situation out of desperation. Frankly, the Western feminist reading of the film makes me wonder if its proponents consider any act by a female character to ever be unjustified.

Cure is fantastic as well, but my (hardly exhaustive) journey through Japanese cinema has not revealed anything that hits quite like Audition. Even Miike's objectively more extreme work, like Visitor Q, don't reach the same richness of texture or depth of commentary by a country mile.

It's certainly disproportionate if you look at it as actions of a single man. What I find really interesting about Audition is its first half, which so many people seem to interpret as perfectly normal, is actually pretty horrifying. The movie does treat it all as normal: that a man might decide, with no real effort put into it, that he deserves to have a second wife. That he might achieve it through women applying for it, and auditioning for it. That he might casually list off the qualifications he wants from a wife at a bar where they simultaneously complain that the women in it are being too noisy. I find the audition itself horrifying, in that it all seemed like no big deal. When it's Asami's turn, the camera is on Aoyama, because it doesn't really matter who she is as a person. The movie sets it up that it's his desires as a man that really matter the most.

The movie casually sets up this banal patriarchy, one where women are practically thought of as being completely abstract figures of desire, their merits reduced down to photos and applications. Asami isn't who Aoyama thinks she is, but also he never really gives a thought to who she really is. Based on an essay and a photo, he just thinks she fits into his ideal of a wife and a mother to his child.

Never mind her trauma. Never mind what she went through because of a societal tendency towards a lack of consequences to the abuse of women. Asami is someone who always fights back. Ask the man who tortured her. Ask the bar owner she once worked for. If anything, Asami can't do enough to tear it all down. She's just fighting back one man at a time.

By the way, I'm an Asian. I was born in Asia, and continue to live here, so I probably don't count as a Western feminist.

I've never watched the film, partially because I read Ryu Murakami's novel it's adapted from, and there's one specific piece of that that I don't think I could stomach seeing on screen if it's there at all.  

Ryu Murakami in general seems to have a theme running through much of his work, dealing with people not being wholly in control of themselves (whether due to outside influences, their own psychology, or what have you), and playing on the dread that comes tied in with that.  I'm not sure I'd categorize it specifically as "man fears" (again though, I'm judging solely by the novel which may not be representative) but admittedly that could be my own bias framing it differently for me.

I always saw it as feminist, myself. The protagonist baits these woman with an audition (which only a gatekeeper can do) as a veil for, as you call it, a personal Tinder. So he’s not just fooling his bride-to-be, but all the other women as well.

Obviously the punishment doesn’t fit the crime at all, but that’s just movie logic. It’s a stylized, extreme film that follows its own rules, not reality. Revenge often equals violence in movies, anyway. We wouldn’t go see Tarantuno if it was called  Incarcate Bill or Prosecute Bill, would we?

How I felt. Both characters are wrong in their own way. And their paths proceed to collide in the worst way. By the end of the film, both inadvertently have gotten exactly what they wanted. Over the top as it might be.

He got someone who truly wanted him. She got someone to say what she always wanted to hear them say.

"Be careful what you wish for" indeed.
I haven't read the novel, but I would be interested in an expansion of that thought. Who is less in control in the novel? From the film, you could make the case either way.

> It's certainly disproportionate if you look at it as actions of a single man. What I find really interesting about Audition is its first half, which so many people seem to interpret as perfectly normal, is actually pretty horrifying. The movie does treat it all as normal: that a man might decide, with no real effort put into it, that he deserves to have a second wife. That he might achieve it through women applying for it, and auditioning for it. That he might casually list off the qualifications he wants from a wife at a bar where they simultaneously complain that the women in it are being too noisy. I find the audition itself horrifying, in that it all seemed like no big deal. When it's Asami's turn, the camera is on Aoyama, because it doesn't really matter who she is as a person. The movie sets it up that it's his desires as a man that really matter the most.

I touched on this a bit above. I haven't really seen people think of that scheme as normal, but now that I think about it in those terms, I think it was abnormal in 1999 (in the same way that it's commonly observed that rom-com male leads do a lot of things that would be looked down upon in real life) and more normal now. They essentially invented Tinder for him, though at least on Tinder everybody knows what they're doing and how it works going in. However underhanded it all was, I don't think the film is trying to use it to get a "you go, girl" reaction from the torture at the end. It's essentially a bad rom-com plot initially conceived to be exactly that, but given new life by the technological horrors we have created since, or at least that's how I saw it.

> The movie casually sets up this banal patriarchy, one where women are practically thought of as being completely abstract figures of desire, their merits reduced down to photos and applications. Asami isn't who Aoyama thinks she is, but also he never really gives a thought to who she really is. Based on an essay and a photo, he just thinks she fits into his ideal of a wife and a mother to his child.

> Never mind her trauma. Never mind what she went through because of a societal tendency towards a lack of consequences to the abuse of women. Asami is someone who always fights back. Ask the man who tortured her. Ask the bar owner she once worked for. If anything, Asami can't do enough to tear it all down. She's just fighting back one man at a time.

I think that the viewer leaning into the feminist reading ultimately hinges on one question: when the needles are being flicked around to the soundtrack of "kiri kiri kiri," and the feet are coming off, are you rooting for Asami? I wasn't, and I doubt that the film wants me to. If you are rooting for Asami, is it still a horror movie?

From what I remember (it has been a couple of years since I read it), the novel kind of plays it both ways.  Both Aoyama and Asami have lost some amount of control over their emotional wellbeing, but because the perspective is centered on Aoyama, we don't know that about Asami until much later.  Aoyama uses the audition process to control the circumstances and limit his own emotional vulnerability.  There's a period of time in the story where it seems like Aoyama has control of the circumstances of their relationship, while Asami has control of the emotional facets of their relationship, but then we learn that Asami's control over her own emotions is more of a mask than it is real.  That reframes their dynamic in such a way that Asami clearly has no control at all, which of course leads to her taking a kind of horrific control over the situation.  So I think ultimately, Asami has less control, both over her circumstances and her emotions, which causes her to exert her will that much more dramatically in the climax, and try to erase Aoyama's personal agency entirely.

I suppose we could approach a gendered reading of the novel with the notion that both men and women suffer emotional hurts, but men more often have the means to protect themselves by controlling the circumstances, while women often do not have the same recourse.  I'm not sure that reading would really bear out (the novel seems to treat Asami as a particular case, rather than representative of women in general), but it's one way to think about it.  I think more so it just kind of explores the way in which that sense of controlling circumstances to protect your emotions can be dialed up to eleven and made horrific.

That's a simplistic binary for horror. You could, in theory, be rooting for Asami, and still be horrified by the things that she's doing. But also, one might not be rooting for *anybody*, and take the film simply as a depiction of a horrible world that inevitably leads to violence.

I just really want to get this clear to you: feminism isn't about rooting for women to kill men. It is about recognizing the systematic means by which society oppresses women, about how patriarchal structures create an environment that minimizes women and their experiences. And hopefully, in recognizing those issues, we can try to fix it. 

A feminist reading of Audition isn't about cheering on Asami as she cuts off this guy's legs. It's about acknowledging how the film exposes the patriarchy, and presents a woman who has been deeply affected by it, creating the conditions for a cycle of violence where no one really wins. At the end, Asami is still a victim, and her "triumph" is still predicated on having been a survivor of violence.

> That's a simplistic binary for horror. You could, in theory, be rooting for Asami, and still be horrified by the things that she's doing. But also, one might not be rooting for anybody, and take the film simply as a depiction of a horrible world that inevitably leads to violence.

Fair, and I already provided my own counterexample to that in the case of I Spit On Your Grave, schlocky as it is.

> I just really want to get this clear to you: feminism isn't about rooting for women to kill men.

Right, we agree on this already, which is why I am arguing that Asami mutilating and murdering men does not itself make the film feminist. You have given that reading additional justification in the rest of your comment, but a mere "comeuppance" reading doesn't move her off the bad guy square at all.

Have you seen Martyrs (the French original)?
